My first job after college was at a call centre in Hyderabad. The trainer told us, "Smile while you talk, even on the phone. Customers can hear it." So I smiled. All day. At the screen, at colleagues, at my manager.
By the third month, I was exhausted. Customers shouted at me. My targets were slipping. But my mouth corners stayed up.
My teammate Mahima kept saying, "You're always so happy, Karthik! How do you do it?"
One evening, walking to the bus, she said it again. And I just stopped smiling. "I'm not happy. I'm really stressed. The smile is part of the job."
She looked shocked. "I had no idea. I thought you were loving it."
"Most days I'm just surviving."
She started checking in after bad calls, asking, "Real smile or work smile?" It helped to have someone who knew the difference.

qa.a: Smile while you talk, even on the phone.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling behind the constant smile by the third month?
qa.a: Karthik felt exhausted and stressed from shouting customers and slipping targets, while keeping a polite work smile.

Manager's note - Harish, marketing team, Monday
Bhavna joined the team six months ago. She's always smiling: in meetings, at her desk, when handed more work. I assumed she was happy with her workload and kept adding projects.
Last Thursday, when I gave her a fourth campaign, she smiled and said, "Sure." But on Friday she sent an email at two in the morning, and on Monday her eyes were red.
I realised I had been reading every smile as "I'm fine."
I asked her for a coffee and said, "I've been giving you a lot. How is the workload, honestly?"
The smile stayed, but her voice shook. "It's too much. I didn't want to seem ungrateful. Smiling is just what I do at work."
I moved one campaign to someone else and set a weekly check-in where she can tell me plainly.
Lesson for me: a smile at work can be politeness, not joy.

qa.a: A fourth campaign.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling behind her smile?
qa.a: Bhavna felt overwhelmed and stressed by the workload, but smiled to seem polite and not ungrateful.

qa.a: He asked honestly about her workload, moved one campaign to someone else, and set a weekly check-in.

Friday
Busiest day of the month at the café. Kishore was on the coffee machine, and every time a customer barked at him, he smiled. Big, bright smile. "Coming right up!"
I used to think he loved this job. He smiles so much.
But today, during the ten-minute break, I saw him in the back, head in his hands, the smile gone. When I came in, it snapped right back up. "Hey, Ritu!"
"Kishore, you don't have to smile at me. It's just us."
He dropped it. "Thanks. My face hurts. Three people complained that their coffee was too hot today. One threw the cup."
"That sounds awful."
"It's fine. It's the job."
We sat for the rest of the break without smiling at all. It felt good, weirdly.
Note to self: a smile at work is often just a uniform.
- Ritu
